To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the activation of the three imatinib-targeted receptors is a common event in chordoma, that it is mediated by the autocrine/ paracrine loop, and that it does not seem to be associated with gene amplification.

the three imatinib mesilate targets, i.e., PDGFRB and its cognate ligand PDGFA, PDGFRA and its cognate PDGFB, and KIT and its cognate stem cell factor, are all activated and expressed in chordoma cells and that the activation of the receptors is due to an autocrine/paracrime loop.
imatinib mesilate is effective against chordomas because of its inhibiting action on the PDGFRB receptor, which is activated by the autocrine/ paracrine loop of PDGFB and PDGFA.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of the molecular mechanisms responsible for imatinib responsiveness in chordomas, and it may be helpful in identifying new molecular targets for the treatment of chordoma patients who do not respond to imatinib.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the clinical response to imatinib in chordoma patients, which is a rare tumor for which no standard treatment exists.
the molecular and biochemical analyses of the three receptor targets of imatinib mesilate, PDGFRB and KIT in chordoma, and PDGFRA in gliomas
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the activation of the PDGFRB pathway in chordomas is a consequence of the presence of PDGF ligand(s) and the activation of PDGFRA and/or KIT receptors.
PDGFR, PDGFRA and, to a lesser extent, KIT are expressed and activated in chordomas and that imatinib mesilate treatment may be beneficial.
the PDGF pathway is activated in chordomas and that imatinib is a promising treatment for these rare and aggressive tumors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PDGFR pathway is activated by autocrine stimulation of the PDGFB/PDGFRB loop, and that the PDGFA/PDGFRB and SCF/KIT loops may also play a role in chordoma pathogenesis.
the activation status of PDGF receptors in chordoma is due to an autocrine/paracrinesignaling loop and not to gene amplification.

the PDGF/PDGFR signaling pathway is activated in the majority of patients and that the clinical responses to imatinibs observed in chordomas are likely to result from the simultaneous inhibition of all three receptors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the activation of the PDGFR pathway is a general mechanism in the development of chordoma, thus opening the way for the development of new therapeutic strategies targeting the pathway.
the presence of a PDGFRB autocrine/paracrinesignaling loop is a potential target for imatinib mesilate treatment in a subset of chordomas.

the presence of the three receptors and their ligands, together with the activation status of PDGF receptor B, PDGF receptor alpha, and KIT receptor, are the main factors responsible for the clinical response to imatinib in patients with chordomas.
